title: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The view that pruning does not kill a rose is expert opinion, not measured (AF-1). One commercial website disagrees, saying cutting back too far "could stress it out or even kill it" (AF-20, Very Low; C-1). Sources disagree on whether "weak" means the whole plant or a single shoot (C-2), and on renovating in one go or in stages (C-4). Newly planted roses are outside this record.

content.heading: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

items.text: Pruning, even hard or badly done, doesn't kill an established rose that is otherwise healthy.
One source says a rose will survive pruning unless it is cut below the ground line.
A weak or slow-growing rose is pruned less hard than a vigorous one. Within a bush, weak shoots are cut back further.
Pruning before the frosts have passed risks frost damage to the new growth and dieback.
Harm from pruning too hard is usually only a short-term setback. One source says the first year after a hard pruning is a recovery year for growth.
An old or neglected rose can be brought back with hard pruning.
My approach to a heavy renovation is to spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Some sources do it all in one go, and I couldn't find a rule for roses on which to choose.
I couldn't find signs, or a waiting time, for judging whether a hard-pruned rose is recovering. If no new growth appears during the growing season, ask your local rose society.
